routes.description: Establish that Christian belief can remain rational by presenting faith as evidence-responsive trust, defending a cumulative historical case for the resurrection, and showing that textual complexity, religious diversity, hiddenness, and morally difficult doctrines admit coherent Christian treatments.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the relevant evidence can reasonably support theism and the resurrection while the principal skeptical challenges remain compatible with a fallible, historically mediated revelation and a relational account of divine purposes.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cumulative Christian explanation remains rationally available after the debate's principal skeptical challenges are incorporated.

centralBridges.description: Define faith as trust responsive to evidence and specify comparative standards for assessing competing worldview explanations.
Connect textual and historical considerations to a cumulative resurrection inference without treating testimony as automatic proof.
Explain how divine communication can operate through culturally situated, fallible authors despite variants, discrepancies, and literary reuse.
Reconcile hiddenness, present commitment, and judgment with a divine aim centered on freely formed relationship and enduring identity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish Christian claims from rival traditions through case-specific evidential comparison rather than mere similarity or exclusivity.
Show that disputed biblical narratives can retain historically relevant cores under culturally informed, non-fundamentalist interpretation.

routes.description: Establish that Christian belief is not rationally sustained when its extraordinary claims depend on contested testimony, culturally developed texts, subjective experience, and interpretive accommodations while comparable traditions and sincere nonbelief lack a non-arbitrary evidential discriminator.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if ordinary evidential standards and viable naturalistic explanations leave resurrection, revelation, and distinctively Christian claims insufficiently supported, especially given hiddenness, textual instability, rival religions, and difficulties surrounding hell and present belief.

motionBridge.description: Show that the available grounds do not adequately distinguish Christian belief from unsupported or naturally explicable alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate why resurrection testimony and associated traditions require stronger support than the cumulative case supplies.
Account for biblical variation, contradiction, composition, and literary dependence through human cultural development without divine agency.
Explain why sincere nonbelief and naturally generated religious experiences challenge claims of accessible divine revelation.
Require a principled evidential basis for privileging Christianity over competing revelations, miracles, and ancient religious patterns.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether hell, postmortem opportunity, and reported flourishing outside religion make present Christian commitment necessary or coherent.
Use historical, archaeological, demographic, and interpretive difficulties to test the evidential value of major biblical narratives.

sections.title: Evidential Faith, Divine Hiddenness, and Religious Experience
sections.rationale: This section tests whether Christian faith is evidence-responsive and whether divine hiddenness, direct-revelation counterexamples, and naturalistic accounts of religious experience undermine rational access to God.

sections.title: Resurrection Inference and Testimonial Evidence
sections.rationale: The resurrection is a defining Christian claim, so the adequacy of cumulative historical reasoning, appearance testimony, martyr traditions, ordinary experience, and competing explanations carries substantial motion-level importance.

sections.title: Scriptural Reliability, Transmission, and Inspiration
sections.rationale: This section addresses whether manuscript variation, early disputes, discrepancies, culturally situated authorship, and literary reuse are compatible with reliable divine communication or favor a wholly human account.

sections.title: Religious Diversity and Ancient Parallels
sections.rationale: Christian rationality depends partly on whether its claims can be distinguished without arbitrariness from rival revelations and from earlier miracle, exaltation, resurrection, and literary traditions.

sections.title: Hell, Human Flourishing, and Biblical History
sections.rationale: Accounts of hell and present communion bear on the practical coherence of belief, while disputes over Exodus and other biblical narratives test how nonliteral interpretation affects Christianity's historical grounding.
